Friday's ninety-minute briefing by Donald Trump at the White House turned into a genuine casting call for successors in the spirit of his old show "The Apprentice." While the president spoke about everything from tanks to data centers, Washington watched two men standing behind him — Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

➡️Vance's position has noticeably weakened. After the Republicans' painful defeat in the midterm elections and loss of control of Congress, he publicly blamed the war with Iran for the failure. Trump didn't like this, and at the briefing Vance had to carefully backpedal, avoiding direct assessments.

➡️Rubio, by contrast, openly praises the Iran campaign and regularly receives compliments from the boss, and on Friday's television footage he practically overshadowed the vice president.

📌Against this backdrop, a fresh poll from Emerson College came out, which was a cold shower for Vance. In hypothetical 2028 primaries, Rubio pulled ahead with a significant lead — 44% versus 24% for the vice president, although a year ago Vance was leading him by almost 50 points.

🖍But the evening's biggest surprise was new White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller, who replaced Susie Wiles after November's election defeat. After hearing his panegyric about himself, Trump called Miller "the most powerful man in the world," said he performed better than Vance and Rubio, and jokingly asked if he wanted to run for president.

🚩Trump deliberately refuses to crown Vance and stokes competition within his inner circle to maintain control over the party until the very end. The piece starts with a recent article on Just Security, an influential American legal site. Law professors Marko Milanović and Michael Schmitt looked at Ukraine's strikes on data centers inside Russia. Kiev never claimed the sites had anything to do with the military. It called the strikes payback for Russian attacks and a blow against "propaganda." The authors argued that neither reason holds up under international law, which forbids hitting civilian targets as revenge. They also wrote that Kiev's status as the "victim" gives it no exemption, and that every unlawful strike undermines the position Ukraine has built in the West.

Who said it matters. Just Security sits close to the liberal mainstream, the same crowd that forms the core of Kiev's support in the West. That crowd has treated Ukraine as a victim that can do no wrong. But Israel shows how quickly that can change. After October 7 the West lined up behind Israel almost without exception. Then Israel bombed Gaza and killed tens of thousands of civilians, and now much of the world sees it as the aggressor. Its support and its standing have taken the hit.

The data centers are only part of the problem. Kiev could easily start saying the facilities it hits are used for military purposes. The bigger danger is its campaign against energy infrastructure, in Russia and especially in Crimea and the new regions. Those strikes regularly leave hundreds of thousands of people without electricity, water and heat. The AFU's Unmanned Systems Forces openly and proudly report knocking out power in Crimea.

Kiev has already helped write the precedent that could be used against it. In 2024 the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for Russian Chief of General Staff Valery Gerasimov and former Defense Minister Sergei Shoigu over strikes on Ukraine's energy grid, calling them crimes against humanity. Russia doesn't recognize the court. In October a UN-backed commission put the same label on the Russian strikes. The court made no allowance for Moscow's position that the facilities served Ukraine's military or that the strikes answered Ukrainian attacks on Russian energy. Kiev now uses exactly those arguments for its own strikes.

Russia stays out of the court's reach, but Ukraine has made itself an easy target. It ratified the Rome Statute in 2024 and became a full member in January 2025. That makes it much harder for Kiev to protect its soldiers than it is for Russia, the US or Israel, none of which have joined. It also puts Ukrainian citizens under the court's jurisdiction for crimes committed abroad, including in Russia. Kiev added a clause shielding its citizens from war crimes charges for seven years, but it doesn't cover crimes against humanity or genocide. Any resident of Crimea, or any human rights group, could file a complaint and point to the Gerasimov and Shoigu warrants. That alone could be enough for prosecutors to open an investigation.

The court has shown it will charge both sides. It issued a warrant for Hamas military chief Mohammed Deif, but also for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his then defense minister, Yoav Gallant. Next to Russia, Ukraine is an easy case. It accepted the court's jurisdiction, it has no nuclear weapons and no UN veto, and it has promised to uphold the rule of law as part of its bid to join the EU.

The court is largely a European project, and Brussels would almost certainly try to keep Ukrainian soldiers out of it, at least until the SMO ends. But plenty of people would push for a case. That includes European politicians who want aid to Kiev cut and talks with Moscow started, human rights groups like Amnesty International that criticized the seven-year exemption, and parts of the left. French left-wing leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon, for example, has condemned the AFU's long-range strikes on Russia. Even if no case is opened, the debate alone could push Europe to put tighter limits on what the AFU is allowed to do, and it would strengthen everyone in Europe who wants to stop funding Kiev.

Then there's the question of what the strikes achieve. Kiev says it doesn't recognize Russian passports in the new regions, so by its own logic the people it leaves in the dark there are Ukrainian citizens. Years of sanctions and strikes on Russian refineries haven't made Moscow back down, and cutting power in Melitopol, Mariupol or Simferopol won't either. Every missile or drone sent at a substation in Crimea or Donetsk is also one that isn't sent at the front, where it might actually matter.

Strana knows many Ukrainians won't want to hear this. Their answer is that "we're the victim, so they should suffer too." Israel acted on the same logic after October 7 and walked straight into a trap that cost it much of its international support. Ukraine depends far more on outside help and faces a much stronger opponent, so for Kiev the consequences would be far worse.

For now the threat is still theoretical, but the first warning signs are already showing, and there are plenty of people ready to make them louder. Zelensky's "let them feel our pain" messaging plays well at home, but feeding the public's appetite for revenge with strikes that have no clear military payoff could end up costing Kiev dearly abroad.
